paper_metadata.title: Who does well after a stroke? The Sydney Stroke Study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used consecutive recruitment from two hospital stroke units with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and a well-described baseline sample. The participation rate was high, and the source population is representative of hospitalized ischemic stroke patients.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Consecutive eligible persons hospitalised for ischaemic stroke were asked to participate... from consecutive admissions over a 38-month period between May 1997 and June 2000 to the inpatient stroke units at Prince of Wales and St George Hospitals in Sydney, Australia
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the source (hospitalized patients) and the specific hospitals and timeframe.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Consecutive eligible persons hospitalised for ischaemic stroke were asked to participate... 205 people met inclusion and exclusion criteria and gave consent for entry into the study.
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment from specialized stroke units is a robust method to minimize selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: over a 38-month period between May 1997 and June 2000
items.reasoning: Specific dates are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: inpatient stroke units at Prince of Wales and St George Hospitals in Sydney, Australia
items.reasoning: Specific hospitals and city are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Exclusion criteria were: age over 85 years; haemorrhagic stroke; transient ischaemic attack; impairment of consciousness persisting for greater than 7 days at time of stroke; inability to give informed consent; insufficient fluency in English... past history of dementia; other neurological diseases known to affect cognition; current alcohol or drug abuse; a retrospective score on the Informant Questionnaire on Cognitive Decline in the Elderly (IQCODE; Jorm, 1994) 3.31
items.reasoning: Detailed clinical and cognitive exclusion criteria are provided, including specific scale cut-offs.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: 205 people met inclusion and exclusion criteria and gave consent for entry into the study.
items.reasoning: The study successfully recruited a large number of eligible consecutive patients.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1. Sociodemographic and clinical comparisons... Age, Sex, Education, NART-R IQ, Marital status, Living with a family member, IQCODE, ADL + IADL, MMSE, Dementia, Apathy, Depression, Stroke characteristics, Vascular risk factors.
items.reasoning: Comprehensive baseline data is provided in Table 1 for both the 'doing well' and 'poorer outcome' groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While there was attrition (from 205 to 125), the authors performed a detailed analysis comparing completers to non-completers at multiple stages, finding no significant differences in key demographic or clinical variables, suggesting the loss was not informative.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: The sample for this study comprised the 125 participants who had complete ADL, IADL and MMSE scales at both time-points... Of the 205 stroke participants recruited at baseline
items.reasoning: The final sample (125) is 61% of the initial 205. While not the ideal 80%, the authors demonstrate that the remaining sample is representative.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: 37 were lost to follow-up (27 due to withdrawal, three died, four relocated outside Sydney, two were uncontactable and one was excluded for baseline dementia/aphasia missed earlier).
items.reasoning: The authors tracked and categorized the reasons for dropout.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: 27 due to withdrawal, three died, four relocated outside Sydney, two were uncontactable
items.reasoning: Specific reasons for attrition are listed.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: there were no significant differences between the 168 who completed the baseline assessment and the 37 who did not with respect to age (t=-1.13, p=0.26), education (t=-1.21, p=0.23) or sex... no significant differences between the 125... and the 43 patients for whom they were not with respect to age, education, gender, MMSE or ADL+IADL score
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly compared those lost to follow-up with those who remained on all key baseline variables.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: those not continuing in the study at baseline had comparable cognitive and functional scores.
items.reasoning: Statistical tests confirmed no significant differences between completers and non-completers.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors (age, IQ, vascular risks, apathy) were measured using validated, standardized instruments (NART-R, AES, SCID-I) by trained personnel. Measurement was consistent across the cohort.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Vascular risk factors (i.e., hypertension, diabetes mellitus...)... Apathy was defined as a score of ≥ 37 on the AES... premorbid intelligence with the National Adult Reading Test-Revised (NART-R)
items.reasoning: All prognostic factors are defined by specific clinical criteria or validated scales.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Trained psychologists had performed all tests... Trained staff scored these [MRI] with good inter-rater (κ scores 0.7–0.9 on various measures) and intra-rater (κ = 0.8 - 0.9) reliability.
items.reasoning: The study used trained professionals and reported reliability for complex measurements like neuroimaging.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Apathy was defined as a score of ≥ 37 on the AES.
items.reasoning: The cut-off for apathy is a standard clinical threshold, not derived from the study's own data distribution.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The remaining 168 eligible people were scheduled for medical/psychiatric and neuropsychological assessments at baseline
items.reasoning: The protocol was standardized for the entire cohort.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: The sample for this study comprised the 125 participants who had complete ADL, IADL and MMSE scales at both time-points.
items.reasoning: The analysis was restricted to those with complete data for the primary variables.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study appears to have used complete case analysis rather than imputation for missing prognostic factor data.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome ('Doing Well') was clearly defined using a combination of cognitive (MMSE) and functional (ADL/IADL) scores. The thresholds were based on established norms and control group data.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: A favourable outcome was defined as having an MMSE score ≥ 28/30 in addition to an ADL + IADL score equal to 14/14 at the follow-up assessment.
items.reasoning: The composite outcome is explicitly defined with specific numerical thresholds.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Functional ability was measured with the ADL (Katz & Akpom, 1976) and IADL (Lawton & Brody, 1969) scales... Global cognitive function was assessed with the MMSE
items.reasoning: The study used the most widely recognized and validated tools for geriatric functional and cognitive assessment.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: scheduled for medical/psychiatric and neuropsychological assessments at baseline and at 12–15 months follow-up.
items.reasoning: All participants underwent the same follow-up protocol.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study identified and measured key confounders (age, IQ, vascular risks). However, the multivariate models were limited by sample size (splitting variables into two models to avoid over-modeling), and baseline dementia could not be included in the regression because it perfectly predicted the 'poorer outcome' group.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Vascular risk factors (i.e., hypertension, diabetes mellitus, myocardial infarction, angina, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, hypercholesterolemia and smoking)... psychiatric history... stroke severity
items.reasoning: A wide range of clinical and demographic confounders were measured.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Vascular risk factors... were recorded.
items.reasoning: While factors are listed, the specific criteria for 'hypertension' or 'smoking' (e.g., pack-years) are not detailed.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Stroke diagnoses were made according to ICD-10 criteria... Severity was established using the European Stroke Scale (ESS)
items.reasoning: Standardized clinical classifications and scales were used.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The remaining 168 eligible people were scheduled for medical/psychiatric and neuropsychological assessments at baseline
items.reasoning: Standardized baseline assessment for all.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods were described.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: This was an observational cohort study; no matching or stratification was used in the design phase for the stroke group.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: To avoid over modelling, the variables sum of vascular risk factors and GDS were tested in two different models with age and NART IQ as covariates.
items.reasoning: Adjustment was performed, but the need to split models due to sample size limitations may have left some residual confounding unaddressed.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical strategy is transparent and appropriate for the data. The authors used multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors and reported both univariate and multivariate results clearly.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The significance of predictors for a favourable outcome was calculated by multivariate logistic regression (predictors entered collectively if not otherwise specified).
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is clearly laid out in the Methods section.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Significant univariate predictors (age, National Adult Reading Test Intelligent Quotient (NART IQ), sum of vascular risk factors, Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) were tested in multivariate logistic regression.
items.reasoning: The authors used a standard approach of moving significant univariate predictors into a multivariate model.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: multivariate logistic regression
items.reasoning: Logistic regression is appropriate for the binary outcome ('Doing Well' vs 'Poorer Outcome').

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1. Sociodemographic and clinical comparisons... [and subsequent text reporting ORs and CIs]
items.reasoning: The authors report on all variables mentioned in the methods, including those that were non-significant (e.g., stroke side, volume).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
